analysis.one_liner: Charges a 0.1% tax on each purchase of stocks, bonds, and derivatives.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 29 House cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a small tax — one-tenth of one percent — on every covered purchase of stocks, bonds, and derivatives. Someone buying $10,000 of stock would pay $10. The tax would fall mainly on high-volume traders, financial firms, and large investors, with the money going to the federal treasury; it exempts initial stock issues and very short-term debt, and requires US shareholders of foreign subsidiaries to pay on those companies' trades.
analysis.who_benefits: The federal treasury, and by extension the general public if Congress later spends the revenue on public programs. Most of the tax would be borne by large financial institutions, hedge funds, and high-frequency trading firms whose business model depends on enormous numbers of transactions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The federal treasury and taxpayers generally

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes a 0.1% excise tax on purchases of stocks, partnership interests, debt securities, and derivatives, raising federal revenue from financial-market transactions. [S2] [S3]

The tax applies to US exchanges, to transactions where the buyer or seller is a US person, and to trades by controlled foreign corporations (paid by their US shareholders), limiting the ability to dodge it through offshore entities. [S3]
Initial issues of securities are exempt, so companies raising money by selling new shares would pay no tax. [S2] [S3]
Short-term debt with a fixed maturity of 100 days or less is exempt, leaving everyday short-term finance largely untaxed. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Buyers in the securities markets — overwhelmingly big financial firms, hedge funds, and other large institutional investors — plus, potentially, small retirement savers to the extent fund companies pass the cost of their own trading through to them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large financial firms and big investors

drawbacks.text: The tax applies to every covered purchase, including purchases made by mutual funds and retirement funds on behalf of ordinary savers, so some of the cost could reach small investors through slightly higher fund trading costs. [S3]

Taxes on each transaction raise the cost of trading, which critics argue reduces market liquidity and could push some trading to foreign exchanges; the bill responds by taxing any transaction with a US party and directing the Treasury Secretary to write rules preventing avoidance, including the use of non-US persons in transactions. [S3]

The bill does not earmark its revenue for any specific purpose, so it changes nothing for ordinary people on its own; its benefit depends entirely on what Congress later chooses to do with the money. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A one-tenth-of-one-percent tax on trades is small for any single investor but adds up quickly against high-volume traders, who bear most of the cost. The main honest objections are that some cost can leak to small savers through fund trading and that the revenue is not earmarked — its value to the public is indirect. On balance, the cost falls mostly on concentrated financial interests and the design addresses the most obvious avoidance routes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Ways and Means Committee for two years without a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on January 15, 2021, with 14 original cosponsors, and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day. [S3] [S5]
Cosponsorship grew to 28 members, all Democrats, but the bill's only recorded action after that was the committee referral. [S4] [S5]
No hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever recorded, and the bill died at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023. [S5] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The securities industry and high-volume trading firms — they never had to pay the tax, because the bill never got a vote. Large investors keep paying nothing on transactions, while the Treasury forgoes the revenue the tax would have raised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wall Street trading firms, which never paid the tax

for.name: 28 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 28 cosponsors were Democrats.

for.name: 13 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction alongside the sponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on January 15, 2021, and took no further recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor consideration during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so the only measurable support is cosponsorship: all 28 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican ever signed on. [S4]

industries.industry: Securities trading firms and high-frequency traders
industries.note: These firms execute enormous numbers of transactions, so a 0.1% tax per purchase would be a real cost to their business model, while the revenue would go to the treasury. Their interest in blocking the tax ran against the public interest in the revenue.

The bill makes exchanges and US brokers the parties responsible for collecting and paying the tax, adding compliance burden, and higher per-trade costs could reduce trading volume they profit from. The bill also directs the Treasury to coordinate with the SEC and CFTC on administration.
Initial issues of securities are exempt, so companies selling new shares to investors pay no tax and fundraising is not discouraged. [S2] [S3]

Fund trades are covered, so small savers could see marginally higher fund costs, though the tax is far larger relative to the profits of the biggest traders than to the trades of a retirement account. [S3]
